revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Surveys and Statistics
revealWordProblem.text: Some sixth-grade students want to get more food choices in the cafeteria. They will conduct a survey of students who buy lunch in the cafeteria. What questions should they include in their survey? Explain your choices.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: A good survey question must be a statistical question — one that anticipates variability, since different students will give different answers. Two strong choices: 'On a scale of 1 to 5, how satisfied are you with the current cafeteria food choices?' and 'Which new lunch item would you most like to see added: pizza, tacos, a salad bar, or stir-fry?' Both work because the answers will differ from student to student and can be tallied — for example, if 45 out of 80 students surveyed pick tacos, that's 45 ÷ 80 = 0.5625 = 56.25% of respondents, showing tacos as the clear favorite to petition for. A question like 'How many days a week does the cafeteria serve lunch?' would NOT belong on the survey, because it has one fixed answer for every student and doesn't anticipate variability.

vocabulary.definition: A statistical question expects varied answers that can be collected as data.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una pregunta estadística espera respuestas variadas que se pueden recopilar como datos.
vocabulary.visual: How many minutes do students in our class read each night?

vocabulary.definition: A question where the answers will be different for different people.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una pregunta cuyas respuestas serán distintas para distintas personas.
vocabulary.visual: “How tall are the players on the team?” → answers vary: 60 in, 63 in, 58 in, 65 in
vocabulary.cloze: A question that expects a variety of answers and is answered by collecting data is a ___.

examples.text: How tall are the students in my class?
examples.why: The answers vary, so data must be collected.

vocabulary.definition: A question that has just one fixed answer that is the same no matter who you ask, so there is no data to collect.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una pregunta que tiene una sola respuesta fija, igual sin importar a quién le preguntes, por lo que no hay datos que recolectar.
vocabulary.visual: “How tall am I?” → one answer: 60 in. Everyone who measures gets the same number.
vocabulary.cloze: A question that has one fixed answer and does not need data collection is a ___.

examples.text: How many days are in a week?
examples.why: The answer is always 7 — it never varies, so there is no data to collect.

examples.text: How tall are the students in my class?
examples.why: Different students have different heights, so the answers vary — that makes it statistical.

vocabulary.definition: Facts and numbers you collect, like answers to a survey.

vocabulary.visual: Player heights: 60 in, 63 in, 58 in, 65 in — four different measurements

vocabulary.definition: How spread out the numbers are.

conceptIntro.heading: Let's build it together — What makes a question a statistical question?
conceptIntro.intro: A statistical question is one you answer by collecting data, and the answers are different for different people or cases. A non-statistical question has just one fixed answer. We'll walk through a worked example, try one together, then you'll try a few with hints right there when you need them.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: If you expect the answers to vary, it is a statistical question.

iDo.title: Watch me
lines: Question 1: "How many points did our top player score last night?" There is one player and one game, so there is one fixed answer, like 18 points.
One answer, no variety, so this is NOT a statistical question.
Question 2: "How many points does each player score per game?" The answers vary: 8, 12, 12, 15, 18, 20, 22.
Because the answers are different for different players, I must collect data. This IS a statistical question.

weDo.title: Let's try together
lines: New question: "How many pets does each student in our class have?" Will every student give the same answer, or different answers?
Some students have 0 pets and others have 2 or 3, so the answers vary. Is this statistical or not statistical?
Now a different question: "How many days are in one week?" Does this have one fixed answer or many?
Sentence frame — say it with me: "The multiples/steps I need are ___ , and the answer is ___ ."

approaching.stem: Which of the following is a statistical question?
choices: How many points did each player score this season?
How many points are scored for a free throw?
What sport does this team play?
How many halves are in a soccer game?
approaching.explanation: "How many points did each player score?" is statistical because different players will have different scores — there is variability in the data.
choiceFeedback: A free throw's points are fixed—does this question ask about variation?
What sport is played doesn't vary—do different people answer this differently?
Halves in a game is a rule—does it change from one observation to another?
hints: Re-read each question and ask: would different people or games give different answers, or is there just one fixed answer?
A statistical question expects variability — many answers that differ. Sort each choice into 'one fixed answer' or 'answers that vary'.
Test one: 'How many halves are in a soccer game?' Every game has the same number — no variability there. Check the other three the same way.
approaching.explanationEs: 3 ÷ 1/4 pregunta: ¿cuántas piezas del tamaño de 1/4 caben en 3? La respuesta es 12, porque cada entero tiene 4 cuartos, y 3 × 4 = 12.
choicesEs: Cuántas piezas de tamaño 1/4 caben en 3
3 grupos de 1/4
3 menos 1/4
hintsEs: Vuelve a leer la expresión: 3 es la cantidad total y 1/4 es el tamaño de una pieza. ¿Qué pregunta podría estar haciendo ese planteamiento?
Dividir entre una fracción hace una pregunta de conteo sobre piezas, no de 'una parte de'. Predice: ¿el resultado debe ser mayor o menor que 3?
Imagina una cinta de 3 pies cortada en piezas de 1/4 de pie. Un pie entero ya tiene 4 de ellas: ¿qué pregunta respondes al contarlas?
approaching.explanationEs: 3 ÷ 1/4 pregunta: ¿cuántas piezas del tamaño de 1/4 caben en 3? La respuesta es 12, porque cada entero tiene 4 cuartos, y 3 × 4 = 12.
approaching.stemEs: ¿Cuál de las siguientes es una pregunta estadística?
approaching.explanationEs: «¿Cuántos puntos anotó cada jugador?» es estadística porque distintos jugadores tendrán puntajes distintos: hay variabilidad en los datos.

approaching.stem: Which question is NOT a statistical question?
choices: How many innings are in a baseball game?
How many home runs did each player hit this year?
How many miles does each runner train per week?
How tall is each player on the basketball team?
approaching.explanation: "How many innings are in a baseball game?" has one fixed answer (9) — no variability. The other questions all produce different answers for different people.
choiceFeedback: Each player hit a different number of home runs—would the answer vary?
Different runners train different miles—would the data vary?
Each player has a different height—would the answers vary?
hints: Careful — this asks for the question that is NOT statistical: the one with a single fixed answer instead of varying data.
For each choice ask: 'Would each player or runner give a different number?' The odd one out is a rule of the game, not data you collect.
Start with 'How tall is each player?' — heights differ player to player, so that one IS statistical. Keep testing until one has just one answer.
approaching.stemEs: ¿Qué expresión significa "cuántas piezas del tamaño de 1/3 hay en 2"?
approaching.explanationEs: Encontrar cuántas piezas del tamaño de 1/3 caben en 2 se representa con 2 ÷ 1/3. La respuesta es 6.
hintsEs: Encuentra los dos papeles: ¿cuál número es el total que se reparte y cuál es el tamaño de cada pieza?
Los planteamientos de división se leen total ÷ tamaño de la pieza. El total siempre va delante del signo ÷.
Aquí el total es 2 y cada pieza es 1/3. Arma la expresión con el total primero y luego compárala con cada opción.
hintsEs.stemEs: ¿Qué expresión significa "cuántas piezas del tamaño de 1/3 hay en 2"?
hintsEs.explanationEs: Encontrar cuántas piezas del tamaño de 1/3 caben en 2 se representa con 2 ÷ 1/3. La respuesta es 6.
hintsEs.stemEs: ¿Cuál pregunta NO es una pregunta estadística?
hintsEs.explanationEs: «¿Cuántas entradas tiene un partido de béisbol?» tiene una sola respuesta fija (9): no hay variabilidad. Las otras preguntas dan respuestas distintas para distintas personas.
choicesEs: ¿Cuántas entradas tiene un partido de béisbol?
¿Cuántos jonrones bateó cada jugador este año?
¿Cuántas millas entrena cada corredor por semana?
¿Cuánto mide cada jugador del equipo de baloncesto?
hintsEs: Cuidado: se pide la pregunta que NO es estadística, la que tiene una sola respuesta fija en lugar de datos que varían.
En cada opción pregunta: '¿daría cada jugador o corredor un número distinto?' La que sobra es una regla del juego, no datos que recolectas.
Empieza con '¿Cuánto mide cada jugador?': las estaturas cambian de jugador a jugador, así que esa SÍ es estadística. Sigue probando hasta hallar una con una sola respuesta.

hintsEs.stem: Why is 'How many hours of sleep did each student get last night?' a statistical question?
choices: Because different students got different amounts of sleep
Because it asks about sleep
Because hours are numbers
Because the answer is always 8 hours
hintsEs.explanation: A statistical question anticipates variability — different students slept different amounts, so the data will vary.
choiceFeedback: Sleep is a topic, not why it's statistical—which choice describes variability?
Hours are numbers, but are they used only in statistical questions?
If everyone slept 8 hours, would this be a statistical question?
hints: The question asks WHY it's statistical — focus on what happens when many students answer, not on the topic of sleep.
Think: if you asked every student how long they slept, would you get one number or many different numbers? That idea is called variability.
Picture asking 5 classmates their sleep hours and listing the numbers. Notice whether the list is all the same or varied — that's the key idea.
hintsEs.stemEs: Una cuerda mide 4 pies de largo. ¿Cuántas piezas de 1/2 pie se pueden cortar de ella?
hintsEs.explanationEs: 4 ÷ 1/2 = 4 × 2 = 8 piezas. Cada pie entero contiene 2 mitades, y 4 × 2 = 8.
choicesEs: 8 pedazos
2 pedazos
4 pedazos
1/2 pedazo
hintsEs: Fíjate en los números: la cuerda mide 4 pies y cada pieza mide 1/2 pie, menos que un pie entero.
Empieza en pequeño: averigua cuántas piezas de 1/2 pie caben en solo 1 pie de cuerda.
Cada pie da 2 piezas de medio pie. Ahora cuenta 2 piezas por pie, pie por pie, a lo largo de los 4 pies de cuerda.

choices.stemEs: Una cuerda mide 4 pies de largo. ¿Cuántas piezas de 1/2 pie se pueden cortar de ella?
choices.explanationEs: 4 ÷ 1/2 = 4 × 2 = 8 piezas. Cada pie entero contiene 2 mitades, y 4 × 2 = 8.

choices.stemEs: ¿Por qué «¿Cuántas horas durmió cada estudiante anoche?» es una pregunta estadística?
choices.explanationEs: Una pregunta estadística anticipa variabilidad: distintos estudiantes durmieron cantidades distintas, así que los datos van a variar.
choicesEs: Porque distintos estudiantes durmieron cantidades distintas
Porque pregunta sobre el sueño
Porque las horas son números
Porque la respuesta siempre es 8 horas
choices.explanation: 6 ÷ 1/5 means how many 1/5-size pieces fit into 6. Each whole has 5 fifths, so 6 × 5 = 30.
choiceFeedback: You multiplied 6 by 1/5 instead of dividing by 1/5. Dividing by a small fraction gives a much bigger answer.
You flipped it backward. Try: each whole has 5 fifths, so 6 wholes have 6 × 5 = 30 fifths.
Dividing by a fraction smaller than 1 gives an answer bigger than you started with, not 1.
hints: 6 ÷ 1/5 asks: how many 1/5-size pieces fit into 6 wholes? Predict first — more or fewer than 6?
Find how many fifths make 1 whole, then use that count for all 6 wholes.
One whole holds 5 fifths. With 6 wholes, count 5 fifths for each whole — set up that multiplication.

hintsEs: 6 ÷ 1/5 pregunta: ¿cuántas piezas de tamaño 1/5 caben en 6 enteros? Predice primero: ¿más o menos de 6?
Averigua cuántos quintos forman 1 entero y luego usa esa cantidad para los 6 enteros.
Un entero tiene 5 quintos. Con 6 enteros, cuenta 5 quintos por cada entero y plantea esa multiplicación.

You flipped it backward. Try: each whole has 5 fifths, so 6 wholes have 6 × 5 = 30 fifths.
Dividing by a fraction smaller than 1 gives an answer bigger than you started with, not 1.
hints: 6 ÷ 1/5 asks: how many 1/5-size pieces fit into 6 wholes? Predict first — more or fewer than 6?
Find how many fifths make 1 whole, then use that count for all 6 wholes.
One whole holds 5 fifths. With 6 wholes, count 5 fifths for each whole — set up that multiplication.
hintsEs.explanationEs: 6 ÷ 1/5 significa cuántas piezas del tamaño de 1/5 caben en 6. Cada entero tiene 5 quintos, así que 6 × 5 = 30.
hintsEs: La pregunta es POR QUÉ es estadística: concéntrate en lo que pasa cuando muchos estudiantes responden, no en el tema del sueño.
Piensa: si le preguntaras a cada estudiante cuánto durmió, ¿obtendrías un número o muchos números distintos? Esa idea se llama variabilidad.
Imagina preguntar a 5 compañeros sus horas de sueño y anotar los números. Fíjate si la lista es toda igual o variada: esa es la idea clave.

hintsEs.title: Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Question
workedExample.work: How tall is each player on the basketball team?
workedExample.workEs: ¿Cuánto mide cada jugador del equipo de básquetbol?

workedExample.label: Student decision
workedExample.work: This is NOT a statistical question.
workedExample.workEs: Esta NO es una pregunta estadística.

workedExample.label: Student reason
workedExample.work: Height is just one number, so every answer will be the same.
workedExample.workEs: La estatura es un solo número, así que todas las respuestas serán iguales.

hintsEs.correctWork: The reason is wrong. The question asks about EACH player, and different players have different heights — for example 58 in, 60 in, 63 in, 65 in. Because the answers vary from player to player, this IS a statistical question.
hints: The word "each" is a clue that you need data from many players.
Ask yourself: will every player give the same height, or different heights?
hintsEs.explanation: The reasoning step claims every answer will be the same, but the question asks about EACH player and players have different heights — 58 in, 60 in, 63 in, 65 in. Because the answers vary from player to player, the question is statistical after all.
hintsEs.explanationEs: El paso del razonamiento dice que todas las respuestas serán iguales, pero la pregunta es por CADA jugador y los jugadores tienen estaturas distintas: 58 in, 60 in, 63 in, 65 in. Como las respuestas varían de un jugador a otro, la pregunta sí es estadística.
hintsEs.correctWorkEs: La razón está mal. La pregunta es sobre CADA jugador, y jugadores distintos tienen estaturas distintas — por ejemplo 58 pulg, 60 pulg, 63 pulg, 65 pulg. Como las respuestas varían de jugador a jugador, esta SÍ es una pregunta estadística.

hintsEs.stem: A coach asks: "How many hours does each athlete on the track team sleep the night before a meet?" Why is this a statistical question?
choices: Because the answers will vary from athlete to athlete
Because it is about sports
Because it has a numerical answer
Because the coach asked it
hintsEs.explanation: A statistical question anticipates variability. Different athletes sleep different amounts, so the data collected will vary.
choiceFeedback: Sports is a topic—what specific part makes this statistical?
Numbers can appear in fixed-answer questions too—why is this different?
Who asks the question doesn't determine if it's statistical—look deeper.
hints: Notice the words 'each athlete' — the coach plans to collect one number from every runner on the team.
Ask: will all athletes report the same hours of sleep? What we call it when collected answers differ is the key to this question.
Imagine the coach's list: 8, 6.5, 9, 7 hours from different athletes. The first step is naming what a changing list like that shows.
hintsEs.stemEs: Un estante mide 5 pies de largo. Cada libro tiene 1/4 de pie de ancho. ¿Cuántos libros caben en el estante? ¿Qué expresión representa esto?
hintsEs.explanationEs: Estás buscando cuántas piezas de 1/4 de pie caben en 5 pies, que es 5 ÷ 1/4 = 5 × 4 = 20 libros.
choicesEs: 5 ÷ 1/4 = 20 libros
1/4 ÷ 5 = 1/20 de libro
hintsEs: Identifica los papeles: 5 pies es el estante completo y 1/4 de pie es el ancho de un libro.
Contar cuántos libros caben significa total ÷ tamaño de la pieza, y el conteo debe ser mayor que 5 porque los libros son delgados.
Cada pie de estante cabe 4 libros. Úsalo para probar qué planteamiento da un conteo que cubra los 5 pies.
hintsEs.stemEs: Un estante mide 5 pies de largo. Cada libro tiene 1/4 de pie de ancho. ¿Cuántos libros caben en el estante? ¿Qué expresión representa esto?
hintsEs.explanationEs: Estás buscando cuántas piezas de 1/4 de pie caben en 5 pies, que es 5 ÷ 1/4 = 5 × 4 = 20 libros.
hintsEs.stemEs: Un entrenador pregunta: «¿Cuántas horas duerme cada atleta del equipo de atletismo la noche antes de una competencia?» ¿Por qué es una pregunta estadística?
hintsEs.explanationEs: Una pregunta estadística anticipa variabilidad. Distintos atletas duermen cantidades distintas, así que los datos recolectados van a variar.
choicesEs: Porque las respuestas variarán de un atleta a otro
Porque es sobre deportes
Porque tiene una respuesta numérica
Porque la hizo el entrenador
hintsEs: Fíjate en las palabras 'cada atleta': el entrenador planea recolectar un número de cada corredor del equipo.
Pregunta: ¿todos los atletas reportarán las mismas horas de sueño? Cómo se llama cuando las respuestas recolectadas difieren es la clave de esta pregunta.
Imagina la lista del entrenador: 8, 6.5, 9, 7 horas de distintos atletas. El primer paso es nombrar lo que muestra una lista que cambia así.

hintsEs.stem: Which of these is a statistical question?
choices: What time is it right now?
How tall are the students in my class?
What is my shoe size?
What is 7 × 8?
hintsEs.explanation: A statistical question anticipates variability — students' heights differ, so the data will vary.
choiceFeedback: What time it is right now doesn't vary—would collecting data help here?
Your shoe size is one fixed measurement—does it vary for different people?
Multiplication has one answer—would this question ever need data?
hints: Three of these have exactly one answer you could look up or compute. Find the one where collecting data from many people makes sense.
For each choice ask: 'If I surveyed my whole class, would I get a list of different numbers?' A statistical question needs that variety.
Test 'What is 7 × 8?' first — it has one answer no matter who you ask, so it can't be statistical. Apply the same test to the rest.
hintsEs.stemEs: ¿Cuál de estas es una pregunta estadística?
hintsEs.explanationEs: Una pregunta estadística anticipa variabilidad: las estaturas de los estudiantes son distintas, así que los datos van a variar.

onLevel.stem: Which of these would collect data that VARIES (making it a statistical question)?
choices: How many days are in one week?
How many siblings does each student in the class have?
How many minutes are in one hour?
What is 12 + 12?
onLevel.explanation: Number of siblings varies from student to student, so the collected data will vary — that makes it statistical. The others each have one fixed answer.
choiceFeedback: Days in a week is constant—does it vary?
Minutes in an hour don't change—does it vary?
12+12 always equals 24—would data vary?
hints: The capital word VARIES is the clue — you need the question whose answers change from student to student.
Check each choice: is it a fact of the calendar, clock, or math (never changes), or a survey where classmates would answer differently?
Start with 'How many days are in one week?' — that never changes, so its data can't vary. Keep testing each choice the same way.
onLevel.stemEs: ¿Cuál de estas recolectaría datos que VARÍAN (lo que la convierte en una pregunta estadística)?

onLevel.stem: The team analyst writes four questions for the scouting report. Which one is a statistical question?

onLevel.explanation: "How many rebounds does each player grab per game?" anticipates variability — different players grab different numbers of rebounds, so you must collect data. The other three each have one fixed answer.

onLevel.title: Level 2 Extension — A Misclassified Scouting Question

workedExample.label: Question
workedExample.work: How many goals did the league's top scorer net this season?
workedExample.workEs: ¿Cuántos goles anotó esta temporada el máximo goleador de la liga?

workedExample.label: Student decision
workedExample.work: This is NOT a statistical question.
workedExample.workEs: Esta NO es una pregunta estadística.

workedExample.label: Student reason
workedExample.work: It names only one player, so there can be no variability in the answers.
workedExample.workEs: Nombra a un solo jugador, así que no puede haber variabilidad en las respuestas.

onLevel.correctWork: The reason is wrong. "This season" covers many games, and the player scores a different number of goals in each game. Because the data varies from game to game, the question DOES anticipate variability — so it IS a statistical question.

onLevel.explanation: The reasoning step assumes that naming one player rules out variability, but 'this season' spans many games and the goal count changes from game to game. Variability can come from many games for a single player, so the question is statistical.

workedExample.label: Student says

onLevel.prompt: Write one statistical question and one non-statistical question about your school's cafeteria. Explain why each question is or is not statistical, and describe what the data would look like for the statistical question.
onLevel.sentenceFrame: Statistical question: ___. This is statistical because ___. The data might look like: ___. Non-statistical question: ___. This is not statistical because ___.
onLevel.hint: Start by thinking of a question where answers would be different for different people.
hints: You need TWO questions about the cafeteria: one where classmates would answer differently, and one with a single fixed answer.
Brainstorm cafeteria data: minutes in line, lunches bought per week. For the non-statistical one, use a fixed fact like the number of tables.
Start your first sentence: 'How many ___ does each student ___?' Using 'each student' builds in variability — then describe the different answers.
onLevel.explanation: The two expressions ask different questions. 6 ÷ 2 shares 6 into 2 equal groups, so each group gets 3. 6 ÷ 1/2 counts how many half-size pieces fit inside 6, and since each whole holds 2 halves, there are 12. Smaller pieces means a bigger count, so dividing by 1/2 gives a larger quotient than dividing by 2.
onLevel.explanationEs: Las dos expresiones hacen preguntas distintas. 6 ÷ 2 reparte 6 en 2 grupos iguales, así que a cada grupo le tocan 3. 6 ÷ 1/2 cuenta cuántas piezas de medio caben dentro de 6 y, como cada entero contiene 2 mitades, hay 12. Piezas más pequeñas significan una cuenta más grande, así que dividir entre 1/2 da un cociente mayor que dividir entre 2.
onLevel.promptEs: Dividir 6 entre 1/2 da 12, pero dividir 6 entre 2 da 3. ¿Cómo puede dividir entre un número más pequeño (1/2) dar una respuesta más grande que dividir entre un número más grande (2)? Explica con un ejemplo de la vida real.
hintsEs: Vuelve a leer ambas: 6 ÷ 2 reparte 6 en 2 grupos iguales, pero 6 ÷ 1/2 cuenta cuántas piezas de medio tamaño caben en 6.
Escoge un objeto real —6 sándwiches repartidos entre 2 personas frente a 6 sándwiches cortados por la mitad— y describe las dos situaciones.
Empieza tu respuesta con la historia de repartir (6 en 2 grupos) y luego explica qué le hace al conteo cortar por la mitad.

onLevel.instructions: Sort each statement: does dividing by the fraction give a result GREATER than the dividend, or LESS than the dividend?
onLevel.hint: Look at the problem. Is it asking 'how many equal shares' or 'how many pieces of this size fit inside'?
hints: Each card already shows the quotient and the dividend — like 5 ÷ 1/3 = 15. Compare those two numbers.
Check the divisor: dividing by a fraction under 1 makes the quotient grow; dividing by a whole number bigger than 1 shrinks it.
Try the first card: 5 ÷ 1/3 = 15. Ask 'is 15 more or less than the dividend 5?' and drag it to that side.
onLevel.explanation: The three cards with unit-fraction divisors — 5 ÷ 1/3 = 15, 8 ÷ 1/2 = 16, and 6 ÷ 1/4 = 24 — all land above their dividend, because pieces smaller than one whole means more of them fit. The three whole-number divisors — 4 ÷ 2 = 2, 10 ÷ 5 = 2, and 12 ÷ 3 = 4 — land below, because splitting into groups larger than one gives each group less than the total. The size of the divisor compared to 1 is what decides the direction.
onLevel.explanationEs: Las tres tarjetas con divisores de fracción unitaria —5 ÷ 1/3 = 15, 8 ÷ 1/2 = 16 y 6 ÷ 1/4 = 24— quedan por encima de su dividendo, porque si las piezas son más pequeñas que un entero, caben más. Los tres divisores que son números enteros —4 ÷ 2 = 2, 10 ÷ 5 = 2 y 12 ÷ 3 = 4— quedan por debajo, porque repartir en grupos mayores que uno le da a cada grupo menos que el total. El tamaño del divisor comparado con 1 es lo que decide la dirección.

hintsEs.explanation: A strong statistical cafeteria question asks about each person, such as 'How many minutes does each student wait in the lunch line?' — the data would be a spread of values like 2, 5, 7, and 11 minutes. A non-statistical one, such as 'How many tables are in the cafeteria?', has a single fixed answer, so there is nothing to collect or compare.
hintsEs.explanationEs: Una buena pregunta estadística sobre la cafetería pregunta por cada persona, como '¿Cuántos minutos espera cada estudiante en la fila del almuerzo?': los datos serían valores variados como 2, 5, 7 y 11 minutos. Una no estadística, como '¿Cuántas mesas hay en la cafetería?', tiene una sola respuesta fija, así que no hay nada que recolectar ni comparar.
hintsEs.promptEs: Escribe una pregunta estadística y una pregunta no estadística sobre la cafetería de tu escuela. Explica por qué cada pregunta es o no es estadística y describe cómo se verían los datos de la pregunta estadística.
hintsEs: Necesitas DOS preguntas sobre la cafetería: una donde los compañeros responderían distinto y otra con una sola respuesta fija.
Piensa en datos de cafetería: minutos en la fila, almuerzos comprados por semana. Para la no estadística, usa un dato fijo como el número de mesas.
Empieza tu primera oración: '¿Cuántos ___ hace cada estudiante ___?' Usar 'cada estudiante' incorpora variabilidad; luego describe las respuestas distintas.

onLevel.commonMistake: A common mistake in Statistical Questions and Data is judging a question by its topic or its numbers instead of its variability. Students see a question about ONE player, ONE game, or ONE fixed fact — like "How many points does the team need to win a game?" — and call it statistical just because it has a number or is about sports. Or they see a question about a single player's whole season, like "How many touchdowns did the quarterback throw this season?", and call it NOT statistical because only one player is named, forgetting that a season covers many games with a different result each time. Both errors skip the real test: will the answers actually differ from case to case (game to game, player to player)? If yes, it is a statistical question; if there is one fixed answer, it is not.

connect.scenario: The school newspaper wants to write a story about the girls' soccer team. A reporter suggests asking: "How many goals has the team scored total?" The editor says they should ask: "How many goals did each player score this season?"
connect.promptQuestion: Which question is statistical? Why would the editor's question give the newspaper more interesting data?
connect.prompt: The reporter's question is ___ because ___. The editor's question is ___ because ___. The editor's question is better for a story because ___.

choices: 'How many goals did each player score this season?'
'How many goals has the team scored total?'
Both are statistical
Neither is statistical
check.explanation: A statistical question anticipates VARIABILITY — different answers from different players. Asking each player's goals produces many different numbers. The team total has exactly one answer.

check.stem: Why is the team total NOT a statistical question?
choices: Because it has exactly one answer, with no variability
Because totals are never useful
Because it is about soccer
Because you cannot count goals
check.explanation: Statistical questions expect a spread of answers. 'What is the total?' has a single fixed answer, so there is no distribution to describe.

check.stem: Which of these is a statistical question?
choices: How tall are the students in my class?
How tall am I?
What is today's date?
How many minutes are in an hour?
check.explanation: Different students have different heights, so that question produces a data set with variability. Each of the others has one fixed answer.

connect.modelAnswer: The reporter's question is NOT statistical — 'how many goals total' has exactly one answer. The editor's question IS statistical, because different players scored different numbers, so it produces a data set with variability. That spread is what makes a story: you can write about the top scorer, the typical player, and how evenly the scoring was shared.
